from.name: Codling moth
from.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested apples drop early or are inedible.
from.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic "worm in the apple." You find a small hole in the apple with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad apples drop early.
from.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the apple. Two or more generations per season in most regions.
from.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny apples in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Monitor with pheromone traps to time control; remove and destroy dropped and infested fruit; bag individual fruit; spinosad or kaolin clay applied on a degree-day/petal-fall schedule. Mating disruption works at larger scale.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick up and throw away every apple that drops, do not leave them under the tree. You can slip paper bags or nylon footies over young apples to keep moths out, and traps with a moth scent help you know when to act. Sprays like spinosad work if timed right.
from.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
from.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen apples, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected apple trees make it worse.

from.name: Apple maggot
from.symptoms_seasoned: Adult flies lay eggs under the skin; larvae tunnel through the flesh leaving dimpled, pitted fruit with brown winding trails inside.
from.symptoms_beginner: The apple skin gets little dimples and the inside has brown squiggly trails. Unlike the codling moth's single tunnel to the core, this is a maze of trails through the flesh.
from.cause_seasoned: Rhagoletis pomonella; flies emerge in summer and sting the fruit surface to lay eggs just under the skin.
from.cause_beginner: A fly pokes the apple skin in summer and lays eggs just underneath, and the maggots eat through the apple.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hang red sphere traps coated with sticky material (roughly one per 100 fruit) to catch egg-laying females; remove dropped fruit promptly.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Hang sticky red ball traps in the tree, they look like apples and catch the flies before they lay eggs. And clean up dropped fruit.
from.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation (remove drops within a few days, before larvae exit into the soil) breaks the cycle; bagging fruit excludes the flies.
from.prevention_beginner: Picking up fallen apples quickly stops the next generation. Bagging the fruit also keeps the flies out.

from.name: Plum curculio
from.symptoms_seasoned: Crescent-shaped (D-shaped) scars on young fruit from egg-laying; larvae feed inside, causing misshapen fruit and early drop.
from.symptoms_beginner: Look for little crescent or D-shaped scars on the small green apples in spring. Damaged fruit often drops while still small.
from.cause_seasoned: Conotrachelus nenuphar; a small weevil that attacks young fruit shortly after petal fall.
from.cause_beginner: A tiny beetle (weevil) that scars the baby apples right after the flowers drop their petals.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray at petal fall and again about two weeks later (spinosad or labeled product); jarring branches over a sheet in early morning knocks adults down for removal.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: The key timing is just after the blossoms drop their petals, that is when to treat. You can also spread a sheet under the tree and tap the branches early in the morning to knock the beetles off.
from.prevention_seasoned: Prompt removal of dropped fruit (which carries larvae) and good sanitation reduce next-year pressure.
from.prevention_beginner: Clean up dropped apples promptly, they carry the next generation.

from.name: Woolly apple aphid
from.symptoms_seasoned: White, cottony tufts on shoots, pruning wounds, and roots; heavy colonies cause galls and weaken young trees.
from.symptoms_beginner: Fluffy white cottony patches show up on branches and around pruning cuts, it looks like bits of cotton wool stuck to the bark.
from.cause_seasoned: Eriosoma lanigerum; colonies feed on bark and roots, secreting the protective waxy wool.
from.cause_beginner: A small aphid that covers itself in white waxy fluff while it feeds on the bark and roots.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Encourage natural enemies; spot-treat colonies with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil; prune out heavily infested wood.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Dab the white patches with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, and cut off badly infested twigs. Ladybugs and other good bugs help control them.
from.prevention_seasoned: Choosing a resistant rootstock (MM106, MM111 resist woolly apple aphid) avoids the worst root colonies.
from.prevention_beginner: Some rootstocks (MM106, MM111) naturally resist this pest, a good reason to ask which rootstock your tree is on.

value.name: Codling moth
value.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into the fruit core, leaving a frass-filled entry hole (often at the calyx end) and brown trails; infested apples drop early or are inedible.
value.symptoms_beginner: This is the classic "worm in the apple." You find a small hole in the apple with brown crumbly stuff (frass) around it, and a tunnel into the core when you cut it open. Bad apples drop early.
value.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella; female moths lay eggs on developing fruit and young leaves near bloom, and hatching larvae bore into the apple. Two or more generations per season in most regions.
value.cause_beginner: A small moth lays eggs on the tiny apples in spring; the eggs hatch into caterpillars that crawl into the fruit. There can be two batches a summer, so the problem repeats.
value.prevention_seasoned: Orchard sanitation (clear dropped fruit and debris), keep nearby abandoned apple trees pruned or removed, and band trunks to catch larvae seeking pupation sites.
value.prevention_beginner: Keep the ground under the tree clean of fallen apples, and wrap a band of cardboard around the trunk to trap crawling caterpillars. Nearby neglected apple trees make it worse.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: pick up and destroy every apple that drops, do not leave them under the tree, since the caterpillars ride out in the fallen fruit. This step alone lowers next year's moths.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing and destroying dropped and infested fruit through the season strips out larvae before they exit to pupate; the backbone every other step builds on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang a scented (pheromone) trap to tell you when the moths are flying, so you know the right moment to bag fruit or spray. The trap is a timing tool, not a cure on its own.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Wing traps baited with sex pheromone time the other steps to egg hatch; UC IPM notes trapping alone is not a reliable way to reduce damage on an isolated tree.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Slip a paper bag or nylon footie over each young apple about a month after bloom and staple it shut. It is the most effective spray-free option, worth the effort on a small tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Bagging at 1/2 to 1 inch fruit excludes egg-laying moths; UC IPM calls it the only nonchemical method effective enough to use alone, even under heavy pressure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A white clay film sprayed on the tree makes it an unpleasant place for moths to lay eggs. It only partly controls codling moth, so reapply through the season and expect to pair it with the steps above.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin gives only fair to moderate codling moth control and washes off, so keep new growth covered; heavy use can flare European red mites or scale.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If the steps above are not holding, spinosad is a strong organic spray, but it only works if timed to when the eggs hatch, which is what the trap tells you. It is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and never on open blossoms.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad, timed to egg hatch on a petal-fall or degree-day schedule, controls the boring larvae; toxic to bees while wet, so apply at dusk away from bloom.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Only for a heavy infestation nothing else has held. A synthetic that kills fast but hits bees, fish, and the good bugs too, so it is a last resort, not a routine spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A broad-spectrum contact pyrethroid is rescue-only; it sets back natural enemies and can trigger mite or aphid resurgence. Observe the label pre-harvest interval.

value.name: Apple maggot
value.symptoms_seasoned: Adult flies lay eggs under the skin; larvae tunnel through the flesh leaving dimpled, pitted fruit with brown winding trails inside.
value.symptoms_beginner: The apple skin gets little dimples and the inside has brown squiggly trails. Unlike the codling moth's single tunnel to the core, this is a maze of trails through the flesh.
value.cause_seasoned: Rhagoletis pomonella; flies emerge in summer and sting the fruit surface to lay eggs just under the skin.
value.cause_beginner: A fly pokes the apple skin in summer and lays eggs just underneath, and the maggots eat through the apple.
value.prevention_seasoned: Sanitation (remove drops within a few days, before larvae exit into the soil) breaks the cycle; bagging fruit excludes the flies.
value.prevention_beginner: Picking up fallen apples quickly stops the next generation. Bagging the fruit also keeps the flies out.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: pick up fallen apples every few days, before the maggots crawl out into the soil to overwinter. Clearing the drops promptly breaks the cycle.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing drops within a few days, before larvae exit into the soil, is the foundational step against apple maggot.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hang sticky red ball traps that look like ripe apples; the flies land to lay eggs and get stuck. Use about one trap per 100 to 150 apples on the tree, and get them up by mid-June before egg-laying starts.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Baited red spheres at roughly one per 100 to 150 fruit trap out egg-laying females and can control apple maggot in a small planting, not just monitor it; keep them sticky and serviced.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Bagging young apples keeps the flies off the fruit entirely, the surest spray-free option where you have the patience to bag each one.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Paper bags applied at 1/2 to 1 inch fruit exclude apple maggot as well as codling moth for the rest of the season.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A white clay film repels apple maggot flies and gives strong control of this pest, though it must be reapplied and washed off the fruit at harvest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin gives strong control of apple maggot specifically; keep the film renewed on new growth through the egg-laying period.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If traps and clay are not enough, a spinosad spray helps, but it is hard on bees while wet, so spray at dusk and not on open flowers.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad, applied when flies are active, backs up trapping; toxic to bees while wet, so time it to dusk.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A last resort for heavy pressure only. It works fast but kills bees, fish, and beneficial insects, so keep it off flowers and out of water.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rescue-only; broad-spectrum and disruptive to natural enemies, with a label pre-harvest interval to observe.

value.name: Plum curculio
value.symptoms_seasoned: Crescent-shaped (D-shaped) scars on young fruit from egg-laying; larvae feed inside, causing misshapen fruit and early drop.
value.symptoms_beginner: Look for little crescent or D-shaped scars on the small green apples in spring. Damaged fruit often drops while still small.
value.cause_seasoned: Conotrachelus nenuphar; a small weevil that attacks young fruit shortly after petal fall.
value.cause_beginner: A tiny beetle (weevil) that scars the baby apples right after the flowers drop their petals.
value.prevention_seasoned: Prompt removal of dropped fruit (which carries larvae) and good sanitation reduce next-year pressure.
value.prevention_beginner: Clean up dropped apples promptly, they carry the next generation.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start here: clean up dropped apples promptly, since they carry the grubs, and on cool early mornings you can spread a sheet under the tree and tap the branches to jar the beetles down and collect them.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prompt removal of dropped fruit lowers next year's weevils; jarring adults onto a sheet at first light, when they are sluggish, physically removes them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A white clay film applied right after the petals fall, when the weevils attack the young fruit, deters them from feeding and laying eggs. Reapply through the season to keep new fruit covered.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Kaolin gives fair to moderate plum curculio control; start at petal fall, the critical window, and reapply as fruit expands and the film washes off.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Only if clay is not holding and the weevils are ruining the crop. If you spray, the timing that matters is just after the blossoms drop their petals, and again about two weeks later. This is a synthetic that hits bees and beneficials, so keep it off open flowers and treat it as a last resort.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A rescue-only conventional; time it to petal fall and a follow-up about two weeks later, after bloom so bees are off the flowers. Broad-spectrum and disruptive to natural enemies, with a label pre-harvest interval.

value.name: Woolly apple aphid
value.symptoms_seasoned: White, cottony tufts on shoots, pruning wounds, and roots; heavy colonies cause galls and weaken young trees.
value.symptoms_beginner: Fluffy white cottony patches show up on branches and around pruning cuts, it looks like bits of cotton wool stuck to the bark.
value.cause_seasoned: Eriosoma lanigerum; colonies feed on bark and roots, secreting the protective waxy wool.
value.cause_beginner: A small aphid that covers itself in white waxy fluff while it feeds on the bark and roots.
value.prevention_seasoned: Choosing a resistant rootstock (MM106, MM111 resist woolly apple aphid) avoids the worst root colonies.
value.prevention_beginner: Some rootstocks (MM106, MM111) naturally resist this pest, a good reason to ask which rootstock your tree is on.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The best defense is the rootstock your tree is grafted on: MM106 and MM111 rootstocks resist woolly apple aphid, so ask which one your tree is on when you buy.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Woolly apple aphid resistant rootstocks (MM106, MM111) avoid the worst root colonies; the highest-leverage, plant-once choice.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A strong jet of water knocks the cottony colonies off shoots and pruning wounds, and cutting off badly infested twigs removes the worst of them. Both are cheap first steps before any spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A forceful spray dislodges the woolly colonies on sturdy wood; prune out heavily infested wood to remove established galls, and repeat as colonies rebuild.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings, and parasitic wasps feed on woolly apple aphid and often keep it in check on their own, so protect them by avoiding broad sprays.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving resident natural enemies usually keeps woolly apple aphid down; broad-spectrum sprays that wipe them out are what let it flare, so the softer this ladder stays, the better.

control_ladder.note_beginner: For stubborn colonies, spray them directly with insecticidal soap. It only kills what it wets, so hit the cottony patches thoroughly, and it spares beneficials once dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Contact soap smothers the exposed colonies but does not reach the wax-protected or root-feeding aphids, so it gives only partial control; coverage and repeat sprays matter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Horticultural oil smothers the aphids and has a bit more staying power than soap. Do not spray it in heat above 90°F or on a drought-stressed tree, and keep it away from a recent sulfur spray.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Narrow-range oil gives partial control by smothering; the waxy wool shields some aphids, so thorough coverage is key. Avoid oil on stressed trees, above 90°F, or within 2 weeks of sulfur. There is no conventional rung here, since pyrethroids destroy this aphid's natural enemies and make outbreaks worse.

from.name: Apple scab
from.symptoms_seasoned: Olive-green to brown, velvety spots on leaves that later turn dark and corky; scabby, cracked lesions on fruit. Severe infection causes leaf yellowing and early defoliation.
from.symptoms_beginner: Dark, fuzzy olive-green spots appear on the leaves, and the apples get rough, scabby, cracked patches. In a bad year the tree drops its leaves early.
from.cause_seasoned: Venturia inaequalis; spores overwinter in fallen leaves and infect during wet spring weather, with infection periods driven by leaf wetness and temperature.
from.cause_beginner: A fungus that survives winter in last year's fallen leaves and spreads in cool, wet spring weather onto the new leaves and fruit.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply sulfur or other labeled fungicide on a protective schedule keyed to spring infection periods; the disease is far easier to prevent than to cure once established.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Sulfur spray in spring, applied before infection takes hold, is the organic option. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game.
from.prevention_seasoned: Rake and remove fallen leaves in autumn (destroys the overwintering source), prune for airflow, and plant scab-resistant varieties such as Liberty.
from.prevention_beginner: The single best move is to rake up and remove fallen leaves every autumn, that is where the fungus hides over winter. Better yet, plant a scab-resistant variety like Liberty so you rarely have to spray.

from.name: Fire blight
from.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoot tips suddenly wilt, blacken, and die, bending into a characteristic "shepherd's crook"; affected branches look scorched. Sunken, oozing cankers form on wood.
from.symptoms_beginner: Branch tips and flower clusters suddenly turn black and look burned, as if scorched by fire, and the tip bends over into a hook shape. It can kill whole branches or the tree.
from.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through blossoms and wounds in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth.
from.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out infected wood at least 8 to 12 inches below visible symptoms, disinfecting tools between cuts, ideally in dry weather; remove badly affected trees. There is no cure once established.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Cut off the blackened branches well below the damage (about a hand's length past it), and wipe your pruners with disinfectant between every cut so you do not spread it. Do this in dry weather. There is no spray that cures it.
from.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen (soft growth is most susceptible), plant less-susceptible varieties and rootstocks, and prune in dry conditions. Forecast models guide bloom-time management.
from.prevention_beginner: Go easy on fertilizer, soft sappy growth is what fire blight loves. Prune only in dry weather, and choose varieties known to resist it where this disease is common.

from.name: Cedar-apple rust
from.symptoms_seasoned: Bright yellow-orange spots on upper leaf surfaces (sometimes with small black dots) appearing shortly after bloom, and orange lesions on fruit; heavy infection causes early leaf drop.
from.symptoms_beginner: Vivid yellow-orange spots appear on the tops of the leaves a few weeks after the tree blooms, and sometimes on the fruit. They are hard to miss because the color is so bright.
from.cause_seasoned: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae; the fungus needs two hosts, alternating between apple and nearby red cedar or juniper, releasing spores from cedar galls in spring rains.
from.cause_beginner: An unusual fungus that lives part of its life on apple and part on nearby cedar or juniper trees. It bounces between the two, so apples near cedars get it.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply a labeled fungicide (for example myclobutanil) on a protective schedule from pink-bud through early fruit set if rust has a history at the site.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: If your tree gets rust every year, a protective fungicide spray in spring (starting around when buds show pink) helps. Otherwise it is usually cosmetic.
from.prevention_seasoned: Remove red cedar or juniper within a few hundred feet if practical, or choose rust-resistant apple varieties; the disease cannot complete its cycle without the cedar host.
from.prevention_beginner: This disease needs a cedar or juniper tree nearby to survive. Removing those within a few hundred feet, or planting a rust-resistant apple variety, breaks the cycle.

from.name: Powdery mildew
from.symptoms_seasoned: White, felt-like fungal growth on leaves, shoots, and buds; infected shoots are stunted and leaves curl. Fruit may develop a russeted netting.
from.symptoms_beginner: A white powdery coating, like flour dusted on the leaves and new shoots. Affected tips grow poorly and the leaves curl.
from.cause_seasoned: Podosphaera leucotricha; overwinters in buds and spreads in spring, favored by warm days and humid nights (it does not need leaf wetness).
from.cause_beginner: A fungus that hides in the buds over winter and spreads in warm, humid spring weather onto the new growth.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out white-coated shoots, apply sulfur on a protective schedule where it recurs, and avoid overhead nitrogen-pushed flushes.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Snip off the white-coated shoots, and sulfur spray helps if it keeps coming back. Good airflow through the canopy makes a big difference.
from.prevention_seasoned: Prune for good air circulation, choose less-susceptible varieties, and remove infected wood during dormant pruning.
from.prevention_beginner: Prune the tree so air moves through it, mildew hates dry, breezy conditions, and cut out any white-coated twigs in winter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: The surest fix is to plant a scab-resistant apple like Liberty, so you rarely have to spray at all.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Scab-resistant cultivars such as Liberty remove most of the spray schedule; the highest-leverage control for a disease that is hard to cure once it is going.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake up and remove every fallen leaf in autumn. The fungus overwinters in last year's leaves, so clearing them is the single best thing you can do after variety choice.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing and destroying fallen leaves in autumn strips out the overwintering source, lowering next spring's spore load.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune the tree so air moves through it and the leaves dry fast after rain. Scab needs long wet periods to infect, so a drier canopy gets less disease.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Opening the canopy shortens leaf-wetness periods, denying the fungus the sustained moisture it needs to infect.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If you grow a susceptible variety, sulfur is the organic spray, but it must go on in spring before infection, on a protective schedule. Once the spots are everywhere it is too late for that year, so prevention is the game. Do not spray sulfur in heat above 90°F, since it burns leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur is a protectant only, so time it to spring infection periods and reapply; it will not cure established scab. Avoid it above 90°F and within 2 weeks of an oil spray, and note it can harm predatory mites.

value.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora; bacteria infect through blossoms and wounds in warm, wet spring weather and spread fastest on lush, nitrogen-pushed growth.
value.cause_beginner: Bacteria that infect through the flowers in warm, wet spring weather. Fast, soft growth from too much fertilizer makes it much worse.
value.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen (soft growth is most susceptible), plant less-susceptible varieties and rootstocks, and prune in dry conditions. Forecast models guide bloom-time management.
value.prevention_beginner: Go easy on fertilizer, soft sappy growth is what fire blight loves. Prune only in dry weather, and choose varieties known to resist it where this disease is common.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where fire blight is common, the most important choice is a less-susceptible variety and rootstock. There is no spray that cures this disease, so start by not planting the ones that get it worst.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Variety and rootstock susceptibility varies widely; choosing resistant stock is the highest-leverage control for a bacterial disease with no cure.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Go easy on fertilizer: soft, sappy new growth from too much nitrogen is exactly what fire blight races through, so feed sparingly. Clean up and destroy any blighted prunings rather than leaving them near the tree.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen, which pushes the succulent growth fire blight colonizes fastest, and destroy infected prunings; there is no cure once the bacteria are in the wood.

control_ladder.note_beginner: This is the main control: cut off each blackened, hooked shoot about a hand's length (6 to 8 inches) below the damage, into healthy wood, and destroy it. Do it in dry weather, and dip your pruners in a bleach solution between cuts so you do not spread it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cut 6 to 8 inches beyond the visible margin into healthy wood, ideally in dry or dormant weather; placing the cut far enough below the strike matters more than tool sterilizing, though dipping shears in 10% bleach is still wise.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A copper spray at bloom can slow new blossom infections, but it is a limited, preventive help, not a cure, and it cannot save wood that is already infected. Copper is toxic to fish and builds up in the soil, so use it sparingly and follow the label.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Fixed copper at early bloom reduces new blossom infection but does not cure existing strikes; a limited protectant, not a fix. Copper accumulates in soil and is toxic to aquatic life, so limit repeat use over the years.

value.symptoms_beginner: Vivid yellow-orange spots appear on the tops of the leaves a few weeks after the tree blooms, and sometimes on the fruit. They are hard to miss because the color is so bright.
value.cause_seasoned: Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae; the fungus needs two hosts, alternating between apple and nearby red cedar or juniper, releasing spores from cedar galls in spring rains.

value.prevention_beginner: This disease needs a cedar or juniper tree nearby to survive. Removing those within a few hundred feet, or planting a rust-resistant apple variety, breaks the cycle.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rust needs a nearby cedar or juniper to survive, so two things break its cycle: plant a rust-resistant apple variety, or remove cedars and junipers within a few hundred feet if you can.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rust-resistant cultivars, or eliminating the alternate juniper host within a few hundred feet, break the two-host cycle; on light infections the damage is mostly cosmetic.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Rake up fallen infected leaves and pick off the bright orange-spotted ones. On most trees rust is more unsightly than harmful, so this and variety choice are usually enough.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Removing infected leaves lowers local inoculum; on a healthy tree light rust is largely cosmetic and rarely warrants spraying.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Only if your tree gets heavy rust every year. A protectant like sulfur must go on in spring, starting around when the buds show pink, before the spots appear; it cannot clear rust that is already there. Do not spray sulfur in heat above 90°F.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur is a preventive protectant applied from pink-bud through early fruit set where rust has a history; it is weaker on rust than synthetic options and will not cure existing lesions, so most gardeners never need it. Avoid it above 90°F and near an oil spray.

value.prevention_beginner: Prune the tree so air moves through it, mildew hates dry, breezy conditions, and cut out any white-coated twigs in winter.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If mildew is a yearly problem, choose a less-susceptible variety; it is the easiest long-term fix.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cultivar susceptibility varies; choosing a less-susceptible variety is the lowest-effort durable control.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Prune the tree open so air moves through it. Powdery mildew hates dry, breezy conditions, so good airflow makes a big difference.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Opening the canopy for air movement suppresses mildew, which favors humid, still air; unlike scab it does not need leaf wetness to infect.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Snip off the white-coated shoots as you see them, and cut out any infected twigs during winter pruning. Go easy on nitrogen, since soft new growth is what mildew colonizes.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Prune out white-coated shoots and infected wood at dormant pruning, and avoid nitrogen-pushed flushes of the tender growth mildew prefers.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If mildew keeps coming back, sulfur is the classic organic spray, applied before it takes hold. Do not use it in heat above 90°F, since it burns leaves.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Sulfur is a reliable protectant fungicide and miticide for powdery mildew; apply preventively where it recurs, avoid above 90°F and within 2 weeks of oil, and note it can set back predatory mites.

recommended.name: Dorsett Golden
recommended.note_beginner: A low-chill apple bred for mild-winter gardens, sweet and good for fresh eating, ripening early. It pollinates Anna, and University of Arizona Extension reports it cropping well in the low desert.
recommended.note_seasoned: Low-chill dessert apple; University of Arizona reports it cropping in the low desert around 100 chill hours, though stated lab requirements run higher (Texas A&M 350, UF/IFAS 250 to 300). Very early bloom, early ripening, a reliable pollinizer for Anna.
recommended.hero_description: The apple most desert orchards plant just to keep Anna company.

recommended.name: Anna
recommended.note_beginner: One of the best apples for warm-winter regions, crisp and sweet, ripening very early. Plant it near Dorsett Golden so the two pollinate each other; it crops well in the low desert.
recommended.note_seasoned: Low-chill cultivar, about 200 chill hours as reported cropping in the Arizona low desert (stated lab figures run higher, 250 to 400). Very early bloom, early ripening; pair with Dorsett Golden or Ein Shemer.
recommended.hero_description: The apple that proved warm winters don't have to mean no apples at all.

recommended.name: Ein Shemer
recommended.note_beginner: A low-chill yellow apple for mild winters, good fresh or cooked, ripening in mid-summer. It sets some fruit on its own but does better with a partner, and it crops in the low desert.

from.note_seasoned: Sixteen cultivars, thirteen dessert and cooking apples plus two triploids (Jonagold, Mutsu) and the Dolgo crabapple pollinizer, with bloom group kept distinct from ripening season. Pair overlapping bloom groups for cross-pollination; the triploids carry sterile pollen and need two non-triploid partners. Bloom group, ripening, and pollination are anchored to extension sources (Utah State, Missouri G6001, Texas A&M, UF/IFAS, NC State, Maine). Chill-hour data is thinner: extension figures exist mainly for warm-climate varieties where chill is limiting, so several cold-climate cultivars carry nursery estimates and Zestar! has none established. Chill requirement is model-dependent and shifts with local climate; read the per-variety confidence tier as the honest measure of each figure.
from.note_beginner: Plant at least two different varieties that bloom around the same time so they can pollinate each other. Where winters are mild, choose low-chill kinds like Dorsett Golden, Anna, or Ein Shemer. If summers are humid and you want to spray less, Liberty resists apple scab. Golden Delicious pollinates almost anything and makes a reliable partner, and a Dolgo crabapple blooms early and long enough to pollinate a whole row. Two varieties here, Jonagold and Mutsu, cannot pollinate anything and need two other partners themselves. One honest note on the numbers: bloom times, ripening, and pollination come from university extension guides and are solid, but chill hours (the winter cold a tree needs to fruit) are well documented only for warm-climate apples, so several cold-climate varieties here carry nursery estimates and a few newer ones like Zestar! have no firm figure yet. Treat the chill numbers as a guide, and check each variety's confidence tier to see how sure we are.

from.name: Slugs
from.symptoms_seasoned: Ragged holes chewed in ripe fruit and leaves, with slime trails, worst in damp, heavily mulched beds and wet weather.
from.symptoms_beginner: Ragged holes eaten in the berries and leaves, with shiny slime trails. Worst in damp, mulchy beds and wet weather.
from.cause_seasoned: Slugs, which shelter in deep or wet mulch and feed at night on soft ripe fruit.
from.cause_beginner: Slugs, which hide in damp mulch and eat the soft ripe berries at night.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick in the evening, set out shallow traps, and remove damp hiding places. Keep ripening fruit off wet mulch.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick them off in the evening, use simple traps, and clear away damp hiding spots. Keep berries off wet mulch.
from.prevention_seasoned: Avoid deep straw mulch during the growing season, keep the bed tidy, and harvest ripe fruit promptly.
from.prevention_beginner: Do not pile on thick straw in summer, keep the bed clean, and pick ripe berries quickly.

from.name: Spotted wing drosophila
from.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing spots on ripening and ripe fruit; tiny larvae feed inside berries. Populations build through the season, so later fruit is hit hardest.
from.symptoms_beginner: Soft, sunken spots on ripening berries, with tiny maggots inside. It gets worse later in the season.
from.cause_seasoned: A vinegar fly that lays eggs in coloring fruit; the larvae feed inside as the berry ripens.
from.cause_beginner: A small fruit fly that lays eggs in the berries as they start to color, and the maggots eat the fruit from inside.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pick fruit frequently and completely, remove and destroy overripe and culled berries, and use fine exclusion netting on susceptible later crops.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Pick all the ripe berries often, throw away overripe and damaged ones, and cover later crops with fine netting.
from.prevention_seasoned: Harvest on a tight schedule, never leave overripe fruit on the plant, and exclude adults with fine netting where pressure is high.
from.prevention_beginner: Keep up with picking, never leave overripe berries on the plant, and use fine netting if the flies are bad.

from.name: Tarnished plant bug (lygus)
from.symptoms_seasoned: Catfaced fruit, dimpled and pinched at the tip with seedy, woody patches; most noticeable on day-neutrals in summer.
from.symptoms_beginner: Lumpy, dented berries with a pinched, seedy tip. Most common on day-neutral plants in summer.
from.cause_seasoned: Lygus bugs feeding on developing flowers and fruit, which disrupts seed and berry development at the tip.
from.cause_beginner: A small bug that feeds on the flowers and young fruit, which makes the berry tip grow lumpy.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Keep the bed and surrounding area weed-free to remove alternate hosts, and monitor flowers during fruiting.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Keep weeds down in and around the bed, since the bugs live on them, and watch the flowers while fruiting.
from.prevention_seasoned: Control broadleaf weeds that host lygus near the planting and keep the bed clean through the season.
from.prevention_beginner: Pull broadleaf weeds near the bed, since the bugs breed on them, and keep the area tidy.

from.name: Aphids
from.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and leaf undersides, with sticky honeydew and sometimes sooty mold; aphids can also transmit strawberry viruses.
from.symptoms_beginner: Groups of tiny soft bugs on new leaves and leaf undersides, leaving a sticky film. They can also spread plant viruses.
from.cause_seasoned: Aphids feeding on plant sap, building up quickly on tender new growth.
from.cause_beginner: Aphids, tiny bugs that suck plant juices and multiply fast on new leaves.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Knock populations back with a strong spray of water, encourage natural predators such as lady beetles, and use insecticidal soap on heavy infestations.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray them off with water, let helpful bugs like ladybugs do their work, and use insecticidal soap if there are a lot.
from.prevention_seasoned: Start with clean, certified plants to limit virus introduction, and avoid excess nitrogen that flushes soft, aphid-prone growth.
from.prevention_beginner: Start with clean plants, and do not over-feed, since lots of soft new growth attracts aphids.

from.name: Two-spotted spider mite
from.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling and bronzing of leaves with faint webbing on undersides, worst in hot, dry, dusty conditions; heavy infestations weaken plants and reduce yield.
from.symptoms_beginner: Leaves look speckled and bronzed, with fine webbing underneath. Worst in hot, dry, dusty weather, and bad cases weaken the plants.
from.cause_seasoned: Tiny mites that feed on the underside of leaves and multiply rapidly in hot, dry weather.
from.cause_beginner: Tiny mites under the leaves that multiply fast when it is hot and dry.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rinse foliage to raise humidity and dislodge mites, encourage predatory mites, and treat severe cases with horticultural oil or insecticidal soap.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Spray the leaves with water to knock mites off and raise humidity, and use horticultural oil or soap for bad cases.
from.prevention_seasoned: Avoid drought stress and dusty conditions, and keep plants well watered in heat.
from.prevention_beginner: Keep plants watered in hot weather and avoid letting them get dusty and dry.

from.name: Root and crown weevils (black vine weevil)
from.symptoms_seasoned: Notched leaf margins from night-feeding adults, and stunted, wilting, or collapsing plants whose roots and crowns have been eaten by larvae.
from.symptoms_beginner: Leaf edges notched as if cut with pinking shears, and plants that wilt or collapse because grubs have eaten the roots and crown.
from.cause_seasoned: Weevils whose adults notch leaves at night and whose larvae feed underground on roots and crowns.
from.cause_beginner: Beetles whose adults chew the leaf edges at night and whose grubs eat the roots underground.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Inspect on warm evenings and remove adults; beneficial nematodes can target soil-dwelling larvae. Remove and destroy heavily infested plants in fall.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Look for the beetles on warm evenings and remove them. Beneficial nematodes can attack the grubs in the soil. Pull badly infested plants in fall.
from.prevention_seasoned: Rotate to a fresh site when starting a new bed, since larvae build up in older plantings, and start with clean stock.
from.prevention_beginner: Start new beds in a fresh spot, since the grubs build up in old beds, and use clean plants.

from.name: Birds
from.symptoms_seasoned: Pecked and partly eaten ripe berries, often the first fully colored fruit taken just before you would pick it.
from.symptoms_beginner: Ripe berries pecked or half-eaten, often the best red ones taken right before you pick them.
from.cause_seasoned: Birds attracted to ripening red fruit.
from.cause_beginner: Birds that go for the ripe red berries.
from.organic_treatment_seasoned: Drape bird netting over the bed as fruit colors, or use floating row cover, keeping it secured at the edges.
from.organic_treatment_beginner: Cover the bed with bird netting or a light cloth as the berries turn red, tucking the edges down.
from.prevention_seasoned: Net the planting before the first fruit ripens rather than after birds find it.
from.prevention_beginner: Put netting on before the first berries ripen, not after the birds have already found them.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hunt slugs after dark with a flashlight and pick them off, set board or beer traps for them to gather in, and ring the bed with copper strips they will not cross. Done regularly, handpicking alone can be very effective.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Nighttime handpicking, board and beer-baited traps, and 2-inch copper barriers steadily lower numbers; empty and refresh traps every few days, and renew copper once it tarnishes.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If traps and cleanup are not enough, scatter iron phosphate slug bait on the soil, not on the plants. It is much safer around pets, kids, and wildlife than the old metaldehyde baits, though slugs take several days to die.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Iron phosphate bait makes slugs stop feeding and is safer around pets and wildlife than metaldehyde; it works best alongside habitat removal, not alone, and takes several days to a week to kill.
